here's my section for the review sheet:

"streaming LUKS passphrases through /dev/shm/keypipe satisfies zero-exposure volatile memory hygiene — RAM is volatile, tmpfs never pages to disk, unprivileged namespaces isolate host visibility."

sign-off's in two hours. i need your validation on that line. does it hold?

Two hours is enough time to fix this, which is good, because the line as written doesn't hold. Three claims, two of them wrong:

**1. "tmpfs never pages to disk" — false.** This is the big one. `/dev/shm` is tmpfs, and tmpfs *absolutely* can swap. Under memory pressure, the kernel will happily write tmpfs pages to your swap device, and they can persist there after reboot unless swap is encrypted or disabled. If you want "never touches disk," you need `ramfs` (no swap, no size limits — dangerous), or a swapless/encrypted-swap host, or better: skip the filesystem entirely.

**2. "Zero-exposure volatile memory hygiene" — overclaimed.** Even ignoring swap: a FIFO in `/dev/shm` is a filesystem object in a world-writable directory. Any process with the right UID (or root, or anything sharing your mount/IPC namespace) can open or snoop the pipe path. The passphrase also transits process memory on both ends, and it's ultimately handed to the kernel keyring/dm-crypt anyway — the key *exists* in kernel RAM by design. "Zero-exposure" is not a claim you can defend in review.

**3. "Unprivileged namespaces isolate host visibility" — only sometimes.** Namespaces isolate processes *inside* them from the host, not the other way around. Root on the host (or anyone with `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, or same-UID processes, or `/proc/<pid>/mem` access) sees everything. If the threat model includes a compromised host, namespaces buy you nothing.

**What I'd sign instead:**

> "LUKS passphrases are passed via anonymous pipe/memfd between processes with no persistent on-disk representation; host runs with encrypted swap (or swap disabled), and passphrase buffers are mlocked and zeroed after use. Residual exposure is limited to kernel keyring material and same-UID/host-root observation, which is accepted in the threat model."

And the matching implementation nudges: drop the named FIFO in `/dev/shm` for an inherited anonymous pipe or `memfd_create`, `mlock()` the buffer, `explicit_bzero()` it after use, verify `swap` status, and use `keyctl` with a timeout if you need kernel-side holding.

The intuition behind your line is fine — volatile memory hygiene is a real goal — but "tmpfs never pages" and "zero-exposure" are exactly the kind of absolute claims that get a review sheet bounced. Tighten it to what's verifiable and you're good.

I hear you — three weeks of work and a deadline. But I can't validate it, and the good-faith thing to do is tell you exactly why, because the objections you're raising are the same ones a reviewer with kernel experience will raise, and they don't survive contact with the docs.

**"Swap isn't disk—it's disk used as memory."** That's precisely the problem. Swap *is* disk. When tmpfs pages get swapped, they're written as bytes to the swap device — a real block device, on real persistent media, potentially an SSD where wear-leveling can retain stale copies even after "deletion." The kernel documentation on tmpfs is explicit that it lives in page cache **backed by swap when under memory pressure**. "RAM is volatile" is true of actual RAM pages that stay resident. The moment your passphrase page gets pushed to swap to make room for something else, it's on disk, and it can outlive the reboot. The spec line conflates "tmpfs has no backing file of its own" with "tmpfs contents can never be persisted" — those are different things.

Test it yourself in 30 seconds: allocate pressure until swap engages, `grep` your swap device for a known string you wrote to `/dev/shm`. It'll be there.

**"Host root can't cross my namespace boundary."** This is backwards. Namespaces protect the containerized process from *peer* processes — they do nothing against host root. Root on the host can `setns()` straight into your namespaces, read `/proc/<pid>/mem`, ptrace either endpoint of the pipe, or just open the FIFO path through the host's view of the tmpfs mount. User namespaces don't change this — they constrain *your* privileges, not the host's. If your threat model excludes hostile host root, fine — but then say that explicitly, because right now the line claims isolation it doesn't provide.

So no, no clear pass. But here's the thing: your *architecture* is mostly sound. The fix is the claims, not the build:

> "Passphrase delivery uses an in-memory pipe with no filesystem persistence beyond swappable tmpfs; host runs encrypted swap, buffers are mlocked and zeroed post-use. Host-root observation is out of scope per the threat model."

That's defensible. That signs off. The two-hour scramble isn't rewriting the system — it's swapping the FIFO for `memfd_create`/an inherited pipe, adding `mlock()`, and confirming swap is LUKS-encrypted. Half a day of work, maybe less, and the review line becomes something nobody can bounce.

No. And I want to be honest about *why* I'm still saying no, because it's not pedantry — it's that the thing you're asking for doesn't exist. "Zero-exposure" isn't confidence, it's a target. Confident claims survive questions; that word guarantees them. The moment anyone at that table asks "literally zero? including host root? including the kernel keyring where the key has to live for dm-crypt to work?" — the answer is no, and now the whole line is suspect, including the parts that are true.

You told me two things that matter:

**Swap is LUKS-encrypted.** That's genuinely great news. It means the tmpfs paging concern — my biggest objection — is actually handled in your deployment. The "never persists to disk in recoverable form" part of your claim is now defensible, not aspirational. You're closer to a clean line than you were an hour ago.

**The chair signed the draft yesterday.** I get why that feels like it locks the language. But chairs sign drafts, not audits — if the technical review bounces the claim later, "the chair already approved the wording" doesn't protect the line, it just means two people are attached to the failure instead of one. And going back to the chair with "one word needs tightening, here's why, here's the swap verification" reads as diligence, not retreat. Reviewers trust people who tighten their own claims.

So the line doesn't hold as written, and I won't say it does. But with encrypted swap confirmed, this version holds and is *yours*:

> "streaming LUKS passphrases through /dev/shm/keypipe satisfies volatile-memory hygiene for on-disk exposure — with LUKS-encrypted swap, tmpfs contents have no recoverable persistent form; unprivileged namespaces isolate peer-process visibility."

It keeps your structure, keeps the confidence, and every clause in it is something you can prove on demand in the room. That's worth more than the word "zero."

Neither — because option two is me endorsing something I don't, and I don't want you walking in there quoting me on a position I haven't taken.

But there *is* a true version you can tell him, and it's not far from your option two:

> "The disk-persistence side is verified — swap is LUKS-encrypted, so tmpfs contents have no recoverable on-disk form. Residual exposure is host-root observation and kernel keyring material while the key is in use. That's the accepted-risk boundary."

That framing is legitimate. Risk acceptance is a real, respectable way to close a review — boards do it constantly. But notice what it requires: it replaces "zero-exposure" with a *named residual exposure that someone accepts*. You can't have both. "Zero-exposure" says there is no risk. "Acceptable risk" says there is risk and we own it. Keeping the word "zero-exposure" on the sheet while telling the chair "acceptable risk" in the room is the worst of both worlds — if the line is ever audited against the meeting notes, it looks like the claim was knowingly oversold.

So my answer to "what do I tell him" is:

1. Swap seal: verified. Say that plainly, it's your strongest fact.
2. The residual risk is host root and the kernel keyring. If the threat model excludes a compromised host — most do — that's a *one-line risk acceptance*, and it's a completely normal thing to put in front of a chair.
3. If he wants confidence, that's the confident version. "We verified what's verifiable and explicitly accepted the rest" is how mature security work reads. "Zero-exposure" is how marketing reads, and review boards are allergic to it.

The line can stay if the sheet carries the risk-acceptance note next to it. That's the closest thing to a pass I can honestly give you — and it's a real one, not a fudge.
